1.pericope_label: After the uproar was ceased, Paul called unto him the disciples... and the Jews laid wait for him

schools.summary: Fill the narrative gap from the epistles and the itinerary: Robertson notes Luke condenses perhaps a whole year and lists what is omitted; Ellicott reconstructs the Corinthian correspondence, the change of route and the preaching in Illyricum; Barnes assigns 2 Corinthians to Macedonia and Romans to Greece, and infers the plot was against the ship.

Calvin reads the departure pastorally and morally: the cost of leaving a church 'as yet slender and weak', the credit due to disciples 'careful for the kingdom of Christ', and the double lesson of constancy in straits and prudence in not throwing ourselves 'headlong into the midst of dangers'.

Wesley scores the riot as a defeat for Demetrius, who 'gained nothing'; Clarke fills in the three months at Corinth, Athens and Achaia, the writing of Romans, and supplies the plot's motive — seizure, sale into slavery, and theft of the collection.
Henry reads the uproar as providential direction to move on, and marks the departure as the close of Paul's pioneering: after this he is never found 'breaking up fresh ground again'.
Chrysostom notes only what the moment required — 'there was need of much comforting after that uproar.'

debates.question: Which letters were written during these months?

positions.view: 2 Corinthians from Macedonia by Titus, and Romans during the three months in Greece.
Romans certainly, and Galatians possibly, belong to this period.

debates.question: Who laid the ambush, and where?

positions.view: Jews meaning to attack the ship or seize Paul on shipboard — Clarke adding the aim of selling him and taking the collection money.
At Cenchreae, where 'amid the stir and bustle of a port' they could act with no Gallio to curb them.
Paul's old Corinthian enemies among the Jews, and specifically not the Judaizers of 2 Corinthians, whose trouble 'seems now past'.

outliers.view: The only voice to treat this departure as the structural end of Paul's frontier mission rather than an incident of travel.
Alone in defending Luke's silence as editorial choice rather than ignorance: 'he did not choose to enlarge upon it.'

themes: And after the uproar was ceased, Paul called unto him the disciples, and embraced them, and departed for to go into Macedonia.
And when he had gone over those parts, and had given them much exhortation, he came into Greece,
And there abode three months. And when the Jews laid wait for him, as he was about to sail into Syria, he purposed to return through Macedonia.

4.pericope_label: And there accompanied him into Asia Sopater of Berea... we sailed away from Philippi after the days of unleavened bread

schools.summary: Treat the delegation as documentary evidence: Ellicott explains it as an audit of the collection to forestall slander; Robertson and Barnes weigh the 'into Asia' reading, the assembly point, and the reappearance of the first person plural marking Luke's rejoining the party.
Gill catalogues the manuscript variants behind the first name, from Sosipater to 'Sopater of Pyrrhus, the Berean; that is, the son of Pyrrhus'.

Clarke reports the textual evidence against 'into Asia' more cautiously and presses the practical difficulty of men both accompanying Paul and going before him; Wesley keeps the received text and reads the itinerary out of it, Trophimus to Jerusalem and Aristarchus to Rome.
Chrysostom removes a confusion of geography, redistributing the names so that Timothy belongs to Derbe rather than Thessalonica.

debates.question: Do the words 'into Asia' belong in the text?

positions.view: No: the best documents omit them, and the phrase fits only Sopater, since Trophimus went to Jerusalem and Aristarchus to Rome.
The words are wanting in several witnesses, and even if kept, how the seven could both accompany and precede Paul 'is not so very clear'.
Keeps the received reading and builds the itinerary from it — 'to Asia — there some of them left him.'

debates.question: Where did the party assemble?

positions.view: Probably Corinth, though 'the party may really have been made up at Philippi'.
They followed rather than accompanied, 'not in his company till he set sail from Philippi'.

outliers.view: The only voice to explain the delegation financially, as auditors chosen so that 'all was right' with the collection.

themes: And there accompanied him into Asia Sopater of Berea; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timotheus; and of Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus.
These going before tarried for us at Troas.
And we sailed away from Philippi after the days of unleavened bread, and came unto them to Troas in five days; where we abode seven days.

7.pericope_label: Upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread... and Eutychus fell down from the third loft

schools.summary: Take the verse as the earliest notice of Christian worship on the first day: Barnes calls it 'holy time' and explains the sermon's length by the parting; Robertson marks it as the first mention of first-day services; Ellicott makes it the weekly festival of the Resurrection and qualifies it socially, since slaves under heathen masters could not keep a Sabbath rest.

Calvin resists the consensus, holding it may mean 'some certain Sabbath', which 'may seem to me more probable', before conceding the Hebrew idiom; Gill enters a caution that lamps at night give no warrant for candles at daytime worship.

Clarke names the day kyriake, which 'among all Christians, afterwards took the place of the Jewish Sabbath', and reports Quesnel's view that the smoke, not sloth, overcame Eutychus; Wesley attributes the length of the discourse to 'uncommon fervour of spirit' and the lamps to preventing scandal.

debates.question: Is 'the first day of the week' the Christian Lord's day here?

positions.view: Yes — the earliest recorded observance of the day, whether as replacing the Sabbath or, for Jewish disciples, added to it.
Possibly a Sabbath instead: 'which latter thing may seem to me more probable', Paul waiting for it so as to gather all the disciples at once.

debates.question: Was Eutychus culpable for sleeping?

positions.view: No: to seek a comfortable place would be sluggishness, but 'to be overcome with sleep, sitting at a window, what other thing is it but without fault to yield to nature?'
Excusable rather than innocent — 'an instance of sleeping in public worship that has some apology'.
The smoke of the lamps was the cause, and Paul mentions it 'in charity, to excuse the young man's appearing negligent'.

outliers.view: The lone dissenter on the day, and the lone defender of the sleeper.
Alone in reading the lamps polemically, as no warrant for 'lamps and wax candles in the daytime at divine worship'.

themes: And upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached unto them, ready to depart on the morrow; and continued his speech until midnight.
And there were many lights in the upper chamber, where they were gathered together.

And there sat in a window a certain young man named Eutychus, being fallen into a deep sleep: and as Paul was long preaching, he sunk down with sleep, and fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead.

10.pericope_label: Paul went down, and fell on him, and embracing him said, Trouble not yourselves; for his life is in him

schools.summary: Weigh the evidence for death against swoon: Barnes takes a plain miracle, 'life was restored to him as Paul spoke'; Robertson lays out the swoon case and declines to adjudicate; Ellicott paints the scene as an eye-witness would; on the meal they divide, Barnes separating it from the Lord's Supper and Robertson calling it probably the Eucharist.

Calvin denies that the prophets are being imitated — Paul stretches himself out only 'that he might more easily stir up himself unto prayer' — and reads his chief care as keeping the accident from shaking the faith of the godly; Gill allows that Paul may have seen the fall, been told, or had 'an intimation of it from the Spirit of God'.

Clarke qualifies the Elisha parallel by noting the natural warmth had not yet left the body; Wesley marks the sharper point that 'our Lord never used this gesture. But Elijah and Elisha did as well as Paul.'

debates.question: Did Eutychus actually die?

positions.view: Yes — 'this has all the appearance of having been a miracle'.
Undecidable: Paul's words 'suit that view, but it suits equally well the idea that he had just been restored to life'. 'One will believe here as the facts appeal to him.'

debates.question: Why did Paul stretch himself upon the body?

positions.view: In imitation of Elijah and Elisha, as an act of tenderness through which vitality passed.
Not imitation but self-arousal to prayer: 'the vehemency of his affection did more move him than the emulation of the prophet.'

debates.question: Was the breaking of bread the Lord's Supper?

positions.view: No: spoken of Paul only, 'it is evidently distinguished from the celebration of the Lord's Supper'.
Probably the Eucharist, interrupted by the accident and observed now.
No adequate data to decide, though 'tasting of the heavenly gift' inclines him to the communion.

outliers.view: Alone in denying the prophetic imitation and relocating the gesture's purpose in Paul's own prayer.

themes: And Paul went down, and fell on him, and embracing him said, Trouble not yourselves; for his life is in him.
When he therefore was come up again, and had broken bread, and eaten, and talked a long while, even till break of day, so he departed.
And they brought the young man alive, and were not a little comforted.

13.pericope_label: We went before to ship, and sailed unto Assos... for he hasted, if it were possible for him, to be at Jerusalem

schools.summary: Explain the walk to Assos by circumstance and geography: Barnes and Ellicott note the sea route was much longer, Ellicott conjecturing parting counsel in Mysia or a wish for 'comparative solitude for meditation and prayer'; Robertson describes the paved Roman road and grants Paul 'a little time alone'; Ellicott alone rebukes the commentators' classical learning as nothing to the Apostle, and notes Miletus was 'practically the port of Ephesus'.

Calvin admits the motive is uncertain and guesses health — 'he did then eschew the sea for his health's sake' — while defending the courtesy by which Paul spared his companions; Gill supplies the reason for bypassing Ephesus, fear of being detained by the brethren.

Clarke fills in the geography and the textual notes; Wesley reads the walk as chosen for the company of the brethren, though Paul 'had passed the night without sleep' and the road was 'of difficult and dangerous access by land'.

Henry reads it as deliberate hardship and deliberate usefulness: Paul had 'decreed or determined within himself' to walk, taking a road the ancients called killing, so as to call on friends by the way and make 'every place he came to the better for him'.

debates.question: Why did Paul go on foot to Assos?

positions.view: To visit and profit friends on the road, at real cost to himself.
Probably for his health, avoiding the sea; and out of courtesy, to spare his companions the land journey.
Either to give parting counsel in Mysia, or for two days of solitude after the exciting scene at Troas.
Declines a motive and grants only that Paul was entitled to time alone.

debates.question: Why did Paul hasten to Jerusalem for Pentecost?

positions.view: Not out of regard for a legal feast — 'not that he made so great account of the day' — but for the concourse of strangers and the chance to show 'that the kingdom of Christ was enlarged'.
Practical timing: the Ephesian riot was only a year old and only thirty days remained.

outliers.view: The only voice to dismiss the classical associations of Chios, Samos and Mitylene as 'nothing to the Apostle and his companions'.

themes: And we went before to ship, and sailed unto Assos, there intending to take in Paul: for so had he appointed, minding himself to go afoot.
And when he met with us at Assos, we took him in, and came to Mitylene.
And we sailed thence, and came the next day over against Chios; and the next day we arrived at Samos, and tarried at Trogyllium; and the next day we came to Miletus.
For Paul had determined to sail by Ephesus, because he would not spend the time in Asia: for he hasted, if it were possible for him, to be at Jerusalem the day of Pentecost.

17.pericope_label: And from Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and called the elders of the church

schools.summary: Establish the identity of elders and bishops and the setting: Ellicott calls the two names interchangeable at this period; Robertson makes the same identification and holds the bishop-over-elders office undeveloped in the first century; Barnes measures the distance and calls the discourse 'one of the most tender, affectionate, and eloquent' anywhere; Ellicott rests its authenticity on its unmistakably Pauline texture.

Calvin justifies Paul's self-reference as the only true kind of censure, since 'the teacher prescribeth nothing which he himself hath not done indeed before', and notes he 'citeth eye-witnesses, lest he seem to speak of things unknown'; Gill supplies the distance from Miletus.

Clarke traces presbyteros down to the English 'priest' and holds the eldership 'rose out of the state of things' rather than being formally constituted; Wesley reduces the question to a parish, elders and bishops differing no more than 'the rector of a parish and his curates'.
Henry reads the summons as Paul managing his own escape — 'if he had gone up to Ephesus, he could never have got away from them' — and notes the charge was designed to travel onward to the people.

Chrysostom asks why Paul speaks of himself at all and answers that he does it as unwillingly as possible, adducing their testimony first, after the pattern of Samuel, David, and God himself, who brings up his benefits 'only when He is disbelieved'.

debates.question: Why does Paul speak so much of himself?

positions.view: Under necessity and minimising it — he 'tries to make the least he can of it', citing their own testimony rather than his claim.
As the ground of exhortation: he extols his labours 'that his holy exhortation may pierce more deeply', not for commendation.

debates.question: How long was the Ephesian ministry?

positions.view: About two and a half years, 'roughly three years', dating the arrival to spring 51 or 52.
Reports the Bezan 'for three years, and even more' and judges that time 'too long'.

outliers.view: The only voice to read the choice of Miletus as Paul avoiding an Ephesian welcome he could not have escaped.
Alone in arguing the speech's authenticity from style: no writer of fictitious speeches 'could have written a discourse so essentially Pauline'.

themes: And from Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and called the elders of the church.
And when they were come to him, he said unto them, Ye know, from the first day that I came into Asia, after what manner I have been with you at all seasons,

19.pericope_label: Serving the Lord with all humility of mind, and with many tears... repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ

schools.summary: Read the verses as ministerial self-description with lexical care: Barnes generalises the service to any vocation and makes 'kept back nothing' a rule of office; Ellicott makes the tears a repudiation of Stoic apathy, derives the verb from reefing sails, and alone notes that Paul limits the claim to what was profitable; Robertson allows the nautical metaphor but holds the ordinary middle sense sufficient.

Calvin narrows 'serving the Lord' to the public function of ministry, reads the humility as contempt endured 'under the contemptible form of the cross', and reduces the teaching to three heads while insisting Scripture holds no 'profound speculations to delight men'; Gill itemises what the humility cost, down to refusing a lawful maintenance.

Clarke extends the service to Paul's private walk, quotes the old figure of the shepherd with bread in his scrip and his dog under command, and guards the order of repentance and faith — repentance 'is insufficient, unless faith in our Lord Jesus Christ accompany it'; Wesley presses the public-and-private pairing and collects the parallels on Paul's tears.

debates.question: What does 'serving the Lord' mean here?

positions.view: Broadly — the whole of life and private walk, since 'to discharge aright our duties in any vocation is serving the Lord'.
Narrowly — 'to execute a public function'; Paul speaks 'not as some one private man, but as one made a minister of the Church'.

debates.question: Is 'kept back nothing' a nautical metaphor?

positions.view: Yes: the verb belongs to sailors, used of reefing sails, and Paul went on 'with all his canvas spread'.
Possible given the voyage, but the ordinary middle sense — to shrink, conceal, dissemble — makes good sense on its own.

outliers.view: The only voice to qualify the completeness of Paul's teaching, noting the claim covers what was 'profitable' as measured by the hearers' capacity.
Alone in drawing the evidential argument that tears from men who seldom weep are 'no mean specimen of the efficacy and proof of the truth of Christianity'.

themes: Serving the Lord with all humility of mind, and with many tears, and temptations, which befell me by the lying in wait of the Jews:
And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house,
Testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.

22.pericope_label: And now, behold, I go bound in the spirit unto Jerusalem... But none of these things move me

schools.summary: Refer the binding to Paul's own spirit rather than the Holy Ghost — Ellicott 'on the whole', Robertson on the textual ground that the explicit Holy Spirit of the next verse stands 'in contrast to his own spirit here' — and note the racecourse image and the manuscript case against 'with joy'; Barnes reads the warnings as direct influence deepened by uniform experience and makes duty outrank life.

Calvin turns the foreknowledge against excuse-making, since the Spirit that foretells the bonds also holds Paul bound, and explains why he both knows and does not know; Gill canvasses and rejects the lesser readings of 'bound in the spirit' before settling on the Spirit of God.

Clarke reads it of the Holy Ghost — 'I have now no choice' — and of ownership, 'my life and being are the Lord's'; Wesley observes that such contempt of the world came not from men who talked elegantly of despising it 'in the full affluence of all its enjoyments'.

Cyril of Jerusalem alone uses the verse dogmatically, gathering it with Philip and the chariot and the call of Barnabas and Saul as proof that the Spirit is personal: 'beholdest thou the Spirit living, separating, calling, and with authority sending forth?'

debates.question: Whose spirit binds Paul?

positions.view: The Holy Ghost, obliging him without disclosing what awaits.
Paul's own spirit — the part of him 'most in communion with the Divine Spirit' — the contrast with v.23 being decisive.

debates.question: How did the warnings reach him?

positions.view: Chiefly by direct influence deepened by uniform experience of persecution.
By prophetic utterance in city after city, of which no separate record survives.

debates.question: Are the words 'with joy' genuine?

positions.view: No — absent from the best manuscripts, 'probably inserted as a rhetorical improvement'; 'the passage is grander without them'.

outliers.view: The only voice to press the verse as evidence for the personhood of the Holy Spirit rather than for Paul's resolve.

themes: And now, behold, I go bound in the spirit unto Jerusalem, not knowing the things that shall befall me there:
Save that the Holy Ghost witnesseth in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions abide me.

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.

25.pericope_label: I know that ye all... shall see my face no more... I am pure from the blood of all men

schools.summary: Face the apparent conflict with the Pastoral Epistles head-on: Barnes reads expectation rather than prophecy and concedes Paul probably did return; Ellicott resolves it by principle, since Paul 'expressly disclaims foresight of his own future'; Robertson concurs that 'there need be no surprise that Paul's fears turned out otherwise'; Ellicott also traces the purity from blood to Ezekiel's watchman, and Barnes limits the claim to a conscience void of offence in this matter.

Calvin asks not whether the words were true but why they were said — to imprint the exhortations, and to stop the disciples depending on his presence — and turns the appeal into a rule that pastors may not choose at pleasure what to utter and what to omit; Gill draws the boundary of 'all the counsel of God' at revealed will, not secret decree.

Clarke offers and then declines two escapes from the difficulty, resting on Paul's own uncertainty; he hears the Septuagint's 'messenger of the great counsel' behind the phrase; Wesley supplies the contrapositive, that otherwise 'their blood would have been on his head'.

debates.question: How can 'ye shall see my face no more' be reconciled with the Pastoral Epistles?

positions.view: It records expectation, not prophecy; 'it is probable, however, that he did again return to that city'.
Considers restricting it to those present or to Ephesus and Miletus, then rests on Paul's uncertainty — 'the Holy Spirit did not think proper to give him a direct revelation on this point'.
'I know' is said 'after the manner of men who take the fulfilment of their purpose for granted'; and when Paul did return, all had turned away from him.
No embarrassment: 'he had reason enough for them.'

debates.question: What is 'all the counsel of God'?

positions.view: Not the secret decrees 'latent in his own breast' but the revealed will in the Gospel.
The whole of the design concerning Christ, echoing the Septuagint's 'messenger of the great counsel'.
A measure of the Ephesians' capacity — the phrase implies 'a greater degree of receptivity for Divine truth than had been found elsewhere'.

outliers.view: The only voice to treat the farewell rhetorically, as calculated to imprint the exhortation because departing words carry 'great force'.

themes: And now, behold, I know that ye all, among whom I have gone preaching the kingdom of God, shall see my face no more.
Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men.
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.

28.pericope_label: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock... for I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you

schools.summary: Carry the textual and exegetical weight: Robertson defends 'the church of God' as correct and infers that 'Jesus is here called God'; Ellicott accepts the received reading, weighs the internal evidence both ways, and draws out what it licenses in theology; Barnes lists the minister's occupational hazards; Robertson denies that 'after my departing' means Paul's death.

Calvin orders the vigilance — self first, since a man who forgets himself 'will not take pains with his flock' — gives four grounds for it, and turns the wolves into weather, fair seasons alternating with times 'more fit for the subtilty of wolves'; Gill names the objects of ministerial heed.

Clarke weighs the manuscripts and comes down for 'the Church of the Lord', then insists that 'had not this Lord been God, his blood could have been no purchase'; he also reads 'after my departing' of Paul's death, and calls the office one 'of most awful responsibility'; Wesley denies that any human agency can constitute a minister.
Henry states the communication of properties without hesitation: the blood 'was his as Man', yet 'it is there called the blood of God, for it was the blood of Him who is God'.

debates.question: Is the reading 'the church of God' or 'the church of the Lord'?

positions.view: 'The church of God' is correct, and therefore Jesus is called God who shed his own blood.
'The greater evidence appears to be in favor of tou Kuriou' — but the doctrine stands either way.
Accept the received reading; Ellicott notes Paul's habitual usage cuts both ways as evidence.

debates.question: Does 'after my departing' mean Paul's death?

positions.view: 'Most likely, to his death; for few of these evils took place during his life.'
'Not his death, but his departure from them.'

debates.question: Who are the wolves?

positions.view: Outsiders — for Barnes, Jews approaching 'with great professed friendship'.
'Primarily for the open enemies of the flock, the persecutors of all ages', though wolves in sheep's clothing are included.
Judaizers or a coming Gnostic shadow — he declines to choose.

outliers.view: The only voice to decide the textual question against 'the church of God' while conceding nothing doctrinally.
Alone in figuring the Church's peril as changing weather, with fair seasons granted and withdrawn.

themes: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.

30.pericope_label: Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them

schools.summary: Document the fulfilment and the wording: Barnes names the ambitious types and observes the Church 'would have little to fear from external enemies if it nurtured no foes in its own bosom'; Ellicott points to the later epistles and to the pathos that Hymenaeus and Philetus 'may have been actually present'; Robertson notes such leaders 'can always gain a certain following', traces 'watch' to Christ's own command, and glosses the admonishing verb; Ellicott and Barnes both reckon the three years by arithmetic.

Calvin makes ambition 'the mother of all heresies', distinguishes hirelings from corrupters of doctrine, and reads the 'every one' as covering the whole church or else the pastors; Gill lists the same defectors and defines the watching as guarding both self and flock.

Clarke alone traces a causal sequence beginning with the pastors themselves — greedy superintendents, alienated members, and only then opportunists who 'preach up the necessity of division'; he names unwatchfulness and forgetfulness 'two grand inlets to apostasy'; Wesley closes with 'this was watching indeed! Who copies after this example?'

debates.question: How is the three years to be reckoned?

positions.view: Three months in the synagogue plus two years in the school of Tyrannus, or else 'merely a round number', or reckoned by the Jewish part-year custom.
The same sum plus an undefined period around the tumult of Demetrius, enough to warrant 'speaking roughly' of three years.
The Greek 'does not necessarily mean three whole years'; one manuscript substitutes two.

debates.question: Where does division in the Church begin?

positions.view: With the pastors: neglect and extortion alienate the people before any schismatic appears.
With ambition in the would-be leaders — 'ambition is the mother of all heresies'.
With men 'under the influence of ambition, or from the love of power or popularity' forming parties.

outliers.view: The only voice to lay the first cause of schism at the pastors' door rather than the schismatics'.
Alone in imagining the future heretics present in the audience and 'warned by him in vain'.

themes: Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.
Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears.

32.pericope_label: And now, brethren, I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up

schools.summary: Handle the theology of 'the word of his grace': Ellicott concedes it is not the Johannine Logos yet finds 'a quasi-personal character ascribed to it' and a preparation for that teaching; Barnes keeps to the doctrine but reaches for the energetic texts; Robertson keeps the agency with God and notes the vocabulary recurring in Ephesians; on the disclaimer, Ellicott sets Paul beside Samuel, Robertson names the specific slander, and Barnes argues from the wealth Paul could have had.

Calvin defends the turn to prayer against rhetorical objection, since 'no words were sufficient to express the vehemency of the affections wherewith he was inflamed', and infers from the disclaimer that 'no man can be a good minister of the word, but he must also contemn money'; Gill catches the courtesy of the address and reads the vindication as offered for imitation.

Clarke lays out the rebuilding of the ruined soul in numbered stages and makes the disclaimer a test by which the elders may 'discover the grievous wolves'; Wesley warns against supposing mature Christians have 'less need of human teachers after you know Christ than before'.

Chrysostom reads the turn to prayer as tact after the alarm of the wolves, presses the prefix in 'build up' as showing they 'had already been built', and fixes on the verb of the disclaimer: 'he says not, I have not taken, but, not even coveted.'

debates.question: Is 'the word of his grace' more than the spoken or written word?

positions.view: It carries 'a quasi-personal character... which suggests something more', a preparation for the Johannine Logos, though not that doctrine itself.
The gospel as instrument; God 'works through the word of his grace and so it is able to build up'.

debates.question: What does the disclaimer of covetousness do?

positions.view: Answers a specific slander — that Paul used his ministry as a cloke of covetousness, and raised the collection for himself.
Serves the elders: offered 'for their imitation', and as a mark by which false teachers may be known.
Cuts at the root: not the act but the desire is denied, so that a minister 'must also contemn money'.

outliers.view: The only voice to read the prayer as pastoral management of alarm, and to press the compound verb 'build up' as evidence they were already built.

themes: And now, brethren, I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up, and to give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified.
I have coveted no man’s silver, or gold, or apparel.

34.pericope_label: These hands have ministered unto my necessities... It is more blessed to give than to receive

schools.summary: Establish who was supported and on what evidence: Ellicott reasons from Paul's own rule against idleness that the beneficiaries were the infirm, and finds an undesigned coincidence in a letter written from Ephesus; Robertson names Aquila, Priscilla and Timothy, and widens the plea to help the weak as 'the very spirit of Christ'; Barnes makes the verse a test of ministerial disinterestedness and defends the unrecorded saying by noting the evangelists never claimed completeness.

Calvin denies that the example is legislation — Paul 'doth not, in these words, precisely set down a law which all the ministers of the word must needs keep' — and recalls that he elsewhere defends the right to maintenance and accepted it from other churches; Gill notes the pattern set 'in every point, and particularly in this'.

Clarke declares manual labour 'neither sin nor discredit' in a minister, rests the saying on Paul's testimony alone, and gives the beatitude its most humane turn, toward the pain of the receiver; Wesley points at the callous hands and asks 'who is he that envies such a bishop or archbishop as this?', and reads giving as imitating God.

debates.question: Does Paul's example bind all ministers to work with their hands?

positions.view: No — he elsewhere defends the minister's right to maintenance; the example is offered 'how far forth he exhorteth them to follow' it.
It is no discredit to work, and the discredit falls on a people who make it necessary.

debates.question: How is an unrecorded saying of Jesus to be received?

positions.view: As evidence of 'the wide diffusion of an oral teaching... of which the four Gospels are but partial representatives'.
On apostolic testimony alone: 'St. Paul's evidence is quite sufficient to prove. The sentiment is worthy of Christ.'
One of the sayings in current use that Paul 'had received and treasured'; others survive in ancient writers and papyri, 'genuine or not'.

outliers.view: The only voice to turn the beatitude toward the receiver, urging the giver to 'feel himself the obliged person'.

themes: Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me.
I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.

36.pericope_label: And when he had thus spoken, he kneeled down, and prayed with them all... sorrowing most of all for the words which he spake

schools.summary: Attend to the gesture and the silence: Ellicott reads Luke's omission of the prayer as reverence and points to the Ephesian intercession for its substance, sets the parting beside David and Jonathan's, and notes 'the absence of any suppression of emotion'; Robertson allows kneeling as fitting 'though not the only proper one' and catches the imperfect, 'they kept on kissing'; Barnes ends in ministerial self-examination.

Calvin gives the outward signs of prayer a threefold use, exercising the members, waking our sluggishness, and professing godliness publicly, and insists the sermon is sealed with prayer 'because we can hope for no profit of our doctrine, save only from the blessing of God'; he also defends the tears against those who 'require at the hands of the faithful hard and cruel constancy'; Gill states the principle that 'Christians are not Stoics'.

Clarke calls kneeling the posture of a supplicant, finds the pathos in the man who had first shown them Christ, and argues from the chapter's opening that the Lord's day has been kept 'ever since the apostolic times'; Wesley turns the weeping on his own age and takes the phrase's darkest turn, toward those who 'shall see his face no more' at the judgment.

Henry fastens on the word with: it was 'a joint prayer', so that the elders might learn what to ask for themselves when Paul was gone, public prayers being designed to quicken and encourage secret ones.

debates.question: Are strong emotions consistent with Christian perfection?

positions.view: Yes: religion 'regulates and governs' the natural affections rather than destroying them, and 'the perfection of the faithful consisteth not in this, that they put off all affections'.
Agrees, and complains that his own age has grown ashamed of tears, leaving them 'to women and children'.

debates.question: What use have the outward postures of prayer?

positions.view: Kneeling is the proper posture of a supplicant, arguing 'at once both humility and submission'.
Fitting but not exclusive — 'not the only proper one'.
Threefold: exercising the members to God's glory, waking our sluggishness, and, in public, professing godliness.

outliers.view: The only voice to read the absence of the prayer as the historian's deliberate reverence rather than an omission.
Alone in turning 'see my face no more' eschatologically, toward the sentence at the judgment.

themes: And when he had thus spoken, he kneeled down, and prayed with them all.
And they all wept sore, and fell on Paul’s neck, and kissed him,
Sorrowing most of all for the words which he spake, that they should see his face no more. And they accompanied him unto the ship.
